portal.title: My systems
portal.subtitle: You can open {{allowed}} systems directly; {{pending}} more need a request.

empty.title: You are not authorised for any system yet
empty.reason: This is not a failure, and there is nothing wrong with your account. The default here is deny: to get into a system there must be a rule that explicitly allows you — and that rule stays in the audit log. You can request access below.

console.title: Console
console.notBuilt: This page is not built yet. The console ships in two stages; Applications and Policies are done.
console.renderCrashReason: This is a defect — not something you did, and not the network. Details are in the browser console. Go back to the overview; other pages are unaffected.
console.notAdminReason: You are signed in, but this account is a regular member. This is not a sign-in failure — signing in again will not change it; an administrator needs to grant you the administrator role. Everyday features live under My systems.

login.title: Sign in
login.subtitle: Sign in to reach the systems you have been granted.
login.headline: One entrance, every system behind it.
login.tagline: One sign-in, path-level authorisation, sessions you can revoke at any time. Legacy systems sit behind the gateway with no code changes.
login.idpHint: You will be redirected to your company identity provider and returned here.
login.noIdp: No company identity provider is connected yet, so only local accounts can sign in. Once one is connected, local accounts should be kept for emergencies only.
login.localHint: Local accounts are for emergencies only and every sign-in is audited separately. Use your company account day to day.

changePwd.title: Change the initial password first
changePwd.why: You are using the bootstrap password. Nothing else works until you change it — the server enforces this too, not just this page.
changePwd.mismatch: The two entries do not match
changePwd.revokeNote: Your other sessions are signed out automatically. If you suspect your account was taken over, this is the step that actually takes it back.

reason.enforced_deny: Locked by an enforced deny (lower-level rules cannot override it)
reason.subject_required: This rule needs your identity or group membership resolved first

apps.intro: Systems behind the gate. Legacy systems that cannot be changed sit behind the gateway; the rest use OIDC or SAML.
apps.showDenied: Shown in the portal as “request required”

empty.title: No system has been onboarded yet
empty.reason: Once onboarded, staff can see it in the portal. Two ways in: applications you can change use OIDC or SAML; legacy ones sit behind the gateway with no code changes.

apps.newDesc: Onboarding only makes this system aware of the application. Who may enter is configured under Policies — with no rules the default is deny, so right after onboarding nobody can get in.
apps.afterCreate: Remember to add an allow rule under Policies, or nobody will get in.
apps.fCodeHint: The value downstream systems are configured with. Lowercase letters, digits, - and _ only. Do not change it once set.
apps.fEnvHint: Use your own values verbatim, e.g. PROD / UAT.

connectCost.oidc: The application supports OIDC itself — least work, but it must support it
connectCost.saml: The application supports SAML itself — common in commercial software
connectCost.gateway: Zero change: traffic goes through the gateway, which injects the signed-in identity as headers
connectCost.formfill: For legacy systems that only have a username/password page: the gateway fills the form for them

apps.fBaseURLHint: Where the portal tile links to. With gateway proxying it is also the upstream address.
apps.fGroupsHint: Decides which section it appears under in the portal, and is what group-scoped rules apply to. Optional.
apps.noGroups: No groups yet — you can leave this empty
apps.groupsUnavailable: Cannot load the group list — that is an API problem, not evidence there are none. Leave it empty for now and set it later.
apps.fShowWhenDenied: Show in the portal as “request access” even without permission
apps.fShowWhenDeniedHint: Unchecked: people without access cannot see that it exists. Checked: everyone can see the system and request access — which publishes your system inventory to all staff. Leave it off for sensitive systems.

notReadyWhy.formfill: The gateway side works, but there is no way to configure the credentials it fills — choosing this returns 503.
notReadyWhy.saml: There is no SAML implementation yet; choosing this leads nowhere. Planned for later.

apps.oidcDesc: The client_id and secret are generated for you. All you need is the redirect URI — it is the one value matched strictly, and a single character off makes the other side reject it with invalid redirect_uri.
apps.fRedirectsHint: One per line. Must match the other system exactly — scheme, port, trailing slash.
apps.createdDesc: Put these two values into the OIDC settings of the target system.
apps.copyFailed: Copy failed — select and copy manually
apps.secretOnce: The secret is shown in clear text only this once. Once you leave this screen it cannot be retrieved — losing it means recreating the client, which invalidates whatever is already configured on the other side.
apps.createdNext: Next, check the issuer and policy under Onboarding.
apps.createdOidcFailed: The app was created, but its OIDC client was not. The app itself is usable — add a client manually under OIDC clients; do not create the app again.
apps.editDesc: Code and connect type cannot be changed: they are what the downstream system has in its config. Changing them gives the other side no warning — it only surfaces the next time someone logs in.
apps.connectLocked: Connect type is {{type}} and cannot be changed here. Switching it would orphan the clients or routes already created — delete those first, then recreate the app.
apps.delDesc: The app is retracted (kept in the database, still auditable). The configuration hanging off it stops working.
apps.delNoDeps: No clients, routes or rules hang off this app. Deleting it affects nothing else.
apps.delDepsUnavailable: Could not compute the impact (the endpoint did not answer). That is not the same as no impact — gateway routes or access rules may still hang off it. Find out before deleting.
apps.delRouteWarn: {{count}} gateway route(s) go with it: those hostnames stop being served within 30 seconds.
apps.delKeepRequests: {{count}} access request(s) point at it and are kept — that is the record of who asked for this access and when.

dep.oidcClients: OIDC client(s) — downstream logins break immediately

policy.order: Three scopes. Order of decision: an enforced deny overrides everything → a more specific subject wins → same subject, more specific scope wins → still tied, deny wins → nothing matched means deny.

empty.title: No policies yet
empty.reason: ⚠️ No policies does not mean open — nothing matched means deny, so right now nobody can get in, including you.

policy.noEnforcedAllow: There is no “enforced allow”: it would be a backdoor nobody can close. To guarantee someone gets in, make sure no deny matches them.
policy.simulateHint: Whether they can actually get in — evaluated against the current policies, nothing is written.
policy.noRuleMatched: No rule matched them, so the default deny applies. This is a decision, not a failed query.

outcome.shadowed: shadowed by a more specific rule
outcome.lost_to_deny: lost to a deny at the same rank

reason.rule: Decided by the highest-precedence matching rule
reason.default_deny: No rule matched → denied by default
reason.enforced_deny: Matched an enforced deny (locked at a higher scope)

scopeHint.global: Rules here apply to every application
scopeHint.group: Applies to every application in one group
scopeHint.app: Applies only to the selected application

policy.subjectIdHint: e.g. a user or group ID
policy.noteHint: e.g. needed for SRE on-call, review 2026-12
policy.enforcedHint: Lower scopes cannot override this. Only available for denies — there is no enforced allow, that would be a backdoor nobody can close.
policy.addHint: “Why this rule exists” is required: in six months it is the only thing anyone can go on.
policy.traceHint_one: {{count}} rule matched them, and it decides:
policy.traceHint_other: {{count}} rules matched them; the first one decides:
policy.shadowedWarning_one: {{count}} rule matched but did not take effect. Whoever wrote it probably believes it is live — these “configured but inert” rules pile up faster than anything else, and they are the number one cause of “I granted access and they still cannot get in” tickets.
policy.shadowedWarning_other: {{count}} rules matched but did not take effect. Whoever wrote them probably believes they are live — these “configured but inert” rules pile up faster than anything else, and they are the number one cause of “I granted access and they still cannot get in” tickets.

sessions.title: My sessions
sessions.intro: Where you are still signed in. See one you do not recognise? Sign it out yourself — waiting for an admin is exactly when the damage happens.

empty.title: No sessions found
empty.reason: That cannot be right — you are using one to read this page. Something is wrong with the request rather than there genuinely being none.

grants.title: My access
grants.intro: What you currently hold, and where it came from.
grants.scopeCaveat: ⚠️ This currently shows temporary elevations only (the ones that came from an approval). Long-lived access from groups and departments has no endpoint yet and is not listed here — so an empty list does not mean you have no access.

empty.title: No temporary elevation is active
empty.reason: Temporary elevations come from an approval and are revoked automatically when they expire. Long-lived access is not shown here (see the note above).

matrix.intro: Who can get into which application — this is the result derived from the rules, not the rules themselves. One person can match a global deny, a group allow and an app-level enforced deny all at once; only running the evaluation tells you the outcome. Click any cell for the full decision chain.
matrix.truncated: Computed for {{shown}} people out of {{total}} in this tenant. Beyond this, export rather than render — a matrix of thousands of rows cannot be read by eye.

empty.title: Nothing to show yet
empty.reason: You need at least one application and one user. Onboard a system under Applications, then add rules under Policies — with no rules the default is deny and the matrix would be all crosses.

audit.intro: Two tables. Access events are every allow/deny the gateway made; change log is who touched the configuration. When something goes wrong, check changes first (who deleted that deny), then events (who got in afterwards).

chain.title: Audit chain integrity

reason.prev_hash_mismatch: does not match the previous entry's hash
reason.content_tampered: this entry's own content was altered
reason.seq_out_of_order: sequence numbers are not contiguous; entries are missing

chain.unavailable: The check did not run — that is an API problem, not evidence of a problem in the log
chain.hint: Each entry carries the hash of the one before it, so altering any entry breaks every link after it. ⚠️ This proves only that tampering is detectable; it does not stop someone deleting a whole span and recomputing the chain. That is what the external anchors below are for — and they only start working once exported outside this system.
chain.ok_one: Verified {{count}} entry; its hash checks out
chain.ok_other: Verified {{count}} entries; every hash links up

emptyEvents.title: No access events yet
emptyEvents.reason: One entry is written every time the gateway allows or denies a request. None at all usually means no traffic has gone through the gateway yet, rather than nothing being recorded — check the connection type under Applications.
emptyEvents.pastEnd: Nothing on this page. Go back a page.

emptyChanges.title: No configuration changes yet
emptyChanges.reason: Editing policies, applications or probes each write an entry. A brand-new environment being empty is expected. ⚠️ Changes made directly in the database leave no trace — which is exactly why the audit chain exists.

resilience.intro: When SSO is down every system is down with it — and the people who could fix it cannot get in either. Two things live here: probing a real login from outside to prove it still works, and a way for named people to get in when SSO itself is unavailable.

probes.title: Login probes
probes.desc: Periodically requests the application's upstream and records whether it answers, how fast, and what failed — so a broken path does not wait for someone to report it. ⚠️ This is reachability probing: it proves the service is alive, not that sign-in works. Credential-based login probing is not built yet, so the account and secret below are stored but currently unused.

empty.title: No probes configured
empty.reason: Once configured, the runner requests this application's upstream at your chosen interval and records whether it answers, how fast, and what failed. Without a probe, a broken path is only found when somebody reports it.

probes.revokeFailed: Revoking did not succeed. That credential is still valid — do not treat it as retired; try again.
probes.fUserHint: An account in the target system. It must be read-only.
probes.fSecretHint: Stored encrypted and never returned by the API — if you mistype it you must re-enter it, you cannot read it back.
probes.fCIDRHint: Required. A probe account is a long-lived credential; leaving the source unrestricted hands out a master key.
probes.fIntervalHint: Minimum 60. Once every 5 minutes is already 288 times a day; tighter than that and legacy systems struggle — a probe that takes down the system it measures is this feature's most ironic failure.
probes.readOnlyWarn: ⚠️ Use a read-only account, never an administrator: the probe holds this credential long-term.
probes.notRunning: ⚠️ Only reachability probing runs today (a request to the upstream to see whether it answers). Probing by actually signing in with the probe account is not implemented — the account and secret are stored but not used.

bg.title: Break-glass codes
bg.desc: One-time codes that work even when SSO itself is unavailable. They grant a way in, not permissions — policy evaluation still applies once inside.
bg.failed: Issuing failed. No codes were produced, so it is safe to retry.
bg.printAndSeal: ⚠️ These are shown once. Print and seal them now — once this page is closed nobody can retrieve them and they must be reissued.

overview.intro: Only things that need someone to act. The top row is problems, the bottom row is scale — every tile opens the matching page.
overview.degraded: These could not be read: {{items}}. They show as “unavailable” rather than 0 — unavailable means we do not know whether there is a problem, not that there is none.
overview.appsWithoutRulesHint: Onboarded but no policy = nobody gets in
overview.probesFailingHint: The login path is already broken
overview.probesNeverRunHint: Configured but never executed — no cover at all
overview.denied24hHint: A sudden rise usually means someone changed a rule

people.intro: Both review and everyday administration happen here: who someone is, which groups they are in, how many sessions are alive, when they last signed in. Accounts marked “never signed in” are the first thing a review should clean up. Local accounts can be created here; accounts from a corporate identity source are created automatically on first sign-in.

empty.title: No people in this tenant
empty.reason: There should be at least one administrator. Seeing this usually means the tenant context is wrong rather than that nobody exists.

emptyGroups.title: No user groups yet
emptyGroups.reason: Groups are what let you grant access to a population rather than a person. With a handful of people individual rules are fine; past that, without groups every new joiner needs the whole set configured again.

people.mustChangeHint: The initial password is flagged “must change”: whoever created the account knows it, so it can do nothing else until the owner changes it.

sessions2.intro: Who is online right now. The first place to look when something happens: an account is compromised, someone left today — you need to see how many sessions they still hold and end them on the spot. Changing policy is not enough; sessions already established do not drop because a rule changed.
sessions2.cannotRevokeSelf: You cannot end your own session — use Sign out instead
sessions2.revokeFailed: The session was not ended and is still live. Retry; if it keeps failing, disable the account instead.

empty.title: Nobody is online
empty.reason: Every session has expired or been ended. Your own is missing too, which usually means the tenant context is wrong — you are reading this page, so at least one session is live.

provider.title: Connection details
provider.desc: These are the lines a downstream system needs — copy them directly. What you see is the value this process is actually running with; a document can go stale, this cannot. The issuer comes from the OAP_ISSUER environment variable set at deploy time and is deliberately not editable here: changing it makes every already-connected downstream fail validation at once.
provider.isLocal: ⚠️ The current issuer is a loopback address. Fine for local work, but a real downstream fetches the keys from inside its own container, where localhost points at itself — this must be a publicly reachable address before serving anyone.
provider.prodChecked: Production mode: this value was validated at startup (https required, no loopback addresses, trailing slash stripped); an invalid value refuses to boot.
provider.devNotChecked: Development mode: startup validation is relaxed. In production mode the variable is mandatory and must be https.

status.intro: Whether the systems you use are reachable right now. These are results from a server-side probe that runs every few minutes, not a check made when you opened this page — which is why every card says when it was measured. ⚠️ It measures reachability (is the service alive), not that sign-in necessarily works.
status.neverChecked: never measured — this says nothing about right now
status.noAccess: You do not currently have access to this system — whether it is up and whether you can get in are two different things.

empty.title: Nothing to show
empty.reason: You do not have access to any system yet, or no applications have been onboarded. Start from “My systems”.

license.intro: The licence state of this installation, which features are available, and how much capacity is left. The installation fingerprint on the right is what you send when requesting a licence.

status.not_licensed: This licence does not cover this product

statusWhy.grace: Features are unaffected, but renew soon — the system turns read-only when the grace period ends.
statusWhy.expired: Write operations are disabled; reads and access decisions are unaffected. Pasting a new activation code restores it immediately.
statusWhy.finger_mismat: Usually a database swap or an environment migration. Features are unaffected during the grace period; request a licence for the new fingerprint.
statusWhy.not_activated: Running as the community edition: features and capacity are as listed below, and configuration remains writable.
statusWhy.not_licensed: The code itself is valid but does not cover this product. Your existing licence is untouched.
statusWhy.lapsed: Too long past the grace period for a renewal to restore it; a new purchase is required.

license.remindSoon: Expires in {{days}} days. A 14-day grace period follows, during which features are unaffected; after that the system turns read-only. You can renew now.
license.remindExpired: Expired {{days}} days ago. Renew soon — past the grace period the system turns read-only, and long past it a new purchase is required.

reason.license_inactive: Unavailable in the current licence state

license.fingerprintDesc: The unique identifier of this environment. Send it to the issuer when requesting or renewing a licence.
license.copyHint: What is shown is truncated; the copy button takes the full value — a licence signed for the truncated version will never match.
license.activateDesc: Paste the full string from the issuer. Leading and trailing whitespace is stripped automatically.
license.activateSafe: A failed activation leaves your existing licence untouched: a code that fails verification is never stored. This action also works while read-only — otherwise an expired system could not rescue itself.
license.badShape: unexpected data shape (the API did not return text)

user.pwdRule: At least 12 characters. Sessions on your other devices are unaffected; end them individually under My sessions if you need to.
user.pwdMismatch: The two new passwords do not match

req.intro: Temporary elevation. Without it, “I need to look at production logs today” leaves only two options: refuse, or grant a permanent rule — and nobody ever comes back to delete permanent rules. Temporary elevation ties the grant to its own expiry.
req.noReason: No reason given — this is the one that will be hardest to explain at review time
req.blockedBy: Blocked by a separation-of-duties rule: {{rule}}. This is not “not this time” — it is not permitted at all; change the request or go through the exception process, resubmitting will not change the outcome.
req.notePlaceholder: Note (recorded in the audit log and visible to the requester)
req.noSelfApprove: You cannot approve your own request (the API refuses it)

decidedBy.blocked: Blocked by policy; nobody reviewed it

pending.title: Nothing waiting for review
pending.reason: Requests appear here when someone submits one. Empty is good news — it does not mean the API is broken.

approved.title: Nothing approved yet
approved.reason: Approved requests stay here with their expiry, so reviews can trace them.

rejected.title: Nothing rejected yet
rejected.reason: Rejections are kept too: a review needs to see which requests were turned down.

blocked.title: Nothing blocked by policy
blocked.reason: Requests stopped by separation-of-duties rules land here. They are separate from manual rejections — these cannot be approved at all.

myreq.intro: Request access to systems you need but do not have. Approved access comes with its own expiry and is revoked automatically — nobody has to remember to clean it up.
myreq.reasonPlaceholder: e.g. investigating GRAF-1234, need that day's dashboards
myreq.reasonWhy: The reason is kept in the audit log alongside the approval — in six months it is the only thing anyone can go on.
myreq.submitted: Submitted and awaiting review. Once approved, the system appears under My systems.
myreq.nothingToRequest: There is nothing to request right now. Either you already have access to everything, or an administrator has not marked the system visible-without-access — in that case you cannot see it exists and need to ask them directly.
myreq.blocked: Blocked by a separation-of-duties rule: {{rule}}. Resubmitting will not change the outcome; change the request or go through the exception process.

empty.title: You have not requested anything yet
empty.reason: Pick a system above to make a request. Approved access expires on its own, so there is nothing to clean up afterwards.

path.intro: Policies decide whether someone gets into a system; this decides which endpoints they may call once inside. Evaluation happens in the gateway, so a proxied legacy system needs no code changes — this is how a system without any notion of roles gets per-endpoint control.
path.pickFirst: Pick an application to see its endpoint rules. Rules are per application; there are no global ones.
path.notGateway: This application is connected via {{type}}, so its traffic does not pass through the gateway — rules configured here will never run. Switch it to gateway proxying or form fill to make them effective.

empty.title: No endpoint rules for this application
empty.reason: ⚠️ No rules means every request is denied. An application-level allow only gets them as far as the gateway; the endpoint layer judges again — and at that point Policies and the access matrix both say “allowed” while every request returns 403. Add a /** allow first, then tighten specific endpoints.

path.fMethodsHint: Comma-separated, e.g. DELETE,PUT. Leave empty for all methods.
path.fPatternHint: End with /** for a subtree (e.g. /api/v1/hosts/**); without /** it is an exact path match. ⚠️ A single * is not supported — /api/* is treated as the literal path “/api/*” and will never match anything. More specific rules win.
path.fNoteHint: In six months this is the only thing anyone can go on.
path.fRequireTicket: Only allow when a ticket reference is supplied
path.simDesc: How the gateway would judge this person calling this endpoint. Nothing is written.
path.simFailed: The simulation did not run — that is an API problem, not evidence of a rule problem.
path.stoppedAtApp: The decision stopped at the application level: they cannot get into this application at all, so endpoint rules were never evaluated. The fix belongs under Policies, not here.
path.noRules: ⚠️ This application has no endpoint rules, so every request is denied (path_default_deny) — even though Policies says the user has access. Use the button below to allow all endpoints first, then tighten them one by one.

oidc.intro: Applications registers the system; this gives it a key that can exchange tokens. Downstream needs the client_id, the client_secret and the three addresses below.
oidc.issuerDesc: Copy these directly. They are the values this process is actually running with — a handbook can be out of date, this cannot.
oidc.noRedirect: No redirect URI — this client cannot complete a login
oidc.fRedirectHint: One per line. Must match exactly what downstream sends, including scheme, port and path — one character off and it is rejected. This is where onboarding most often stalls.
oidc.fPublicHint: Only for browser or mobile apps that cannot keep a secret; they use PKCE instead. Do not tick it for server-side applications — that throws away a layer of protection for nothing.
oidc.secretOnce: ⚠️ The client_secret is shown once. Copy it now — only a hash is stored, so once this closes nobody can retrieve it and the client must be recreated.

empty.title: No OIDC clients yet
empty.reason: Applications connected via OIDC need a client here before anyone can actually sign in. Gateway-proxied applications do not.

oidc.clientIDAuto: Generated on create (client_ prefix + 22 random chars) and shown once afterwards.

groups.title: Application groups
groups.desc: A group is two things at once: a section in the portal, and the target of group-scoped authorization rules. An application appears only under its primary group.
groups.none: No groups yet. Applications do not need one — ungrouped applications appear under “Other” in the portal.
groups.unavailable: Cannot load the group list — that is an API problem, not evidence there are none. Do not create one blindly; the code may collide.
groups.impactNone: No authorization rules target this group; deleting it only changes portal sections.
groups.impactSome: ⚠️ {{n}} authorization rules target this group and will be deleted with it — everyone matched by them loses access immediately.
groups.impactUnavailable: The impact could not be determined, so deletion is disabled. The whole point of this dialog is to show you the cost first — deleting without it is changing access blindfolded.
groups.deleteFailed: Deletion did not succeed. The group and its rules are still there; you can retry.

sec.intro: Two-factor authentication: besides your password, a six-digit code generated on your phone. Most compromised passwords belong to ordinary accounts, so this matters for everyone, not just administrators.
sec.whyBind: Once enrolled, signing in and some high-risk actions ask for the six-digit code from your authenticator. Any authenticator works (Google Authenticator, 1Password, Authy…).
sec.step1: 1. Add this secret to your authenticator app by hand
sec.secretHint: No QR code on purpose: typing the secret works just as well, and pulling in a library for one QR code is not worth it. The secret is case-sensitive.
sec.step2: 2. Enter the six digits your authenticator shows right now
sec.confirmWhy: Enrolment only counts once a code has been verified. If showing the secret were enough, a mis-scanned entry or a clock skew would go unnoticed until the next time you actually need it — usually the worst possible moment.
sec.rebindHint: Already enrolled. There is deliberately no “re-enrol” button here — re-enrolling invalidates the old secret immediately, so one stray click would lock you out next time. To move to a new device, ask an administrator to reset it; that path has human confirmation and an audit trail.

idp.intro: Connect a corporate identity source (Lark, Microsoft Teams, or any standard OIDC provider) so staff sign in with their company account instead of yet another password.
idp.unverified: ⚠️ Configuration saves and the login code is in place, but this path has never been exercised with a real account. “Switched on” below means exactly that — not that sign-in works. Once a test account exists, walk the whole path: redirect, callback, user creation, and whether the claims come back as expected.
idp.presetHint: Presets only fill claim mappings and scopes; the secret and endpoints are still yours to enter.
idp.fSecretNew: Required. Stored encrypted and never returned by any API.
idp.fSecretKeep: Leave empty to keep the current one.
idp.discoverHint: Fills the three endpoints below from the issuer's discovery document. Lark does not publish a standard one, so enter those by hand.
idp.fSubjectHint: ⚠️ Do not use email. Change an address and the person becomes someone else, breaking every historical audit link. Entra uses oid; Lark uses union_id.
idp.fRedirectHint: Must match what is registered upstream exactly; one character off and it is rejected.
idp.fJITHint: Off by default. With it on, everyone in the upstream directory — contractors, un-offboarded leavers, test accounts — grows an account here the first time they click through. Being able to sign in is not the same as deserving access: accounts created this way belong to no group, and therefore are denied by default.
idp.fEnabled: Enabled (show this button on the sign-in page)

empty.title: No identity source connected
empty.reason: You do not need one: local accounts work as they are. Connecting one lets staff sign in with their company account, saves a password, and lets access follow upstream offboarding.

anchor.title: External anchors
anchor.noKey: No anchor private key configured (OAP_ANCHOR_KEY), so nothing is being anchored. The hash chain still detects a changed or deleted entry, but not a whole chain recomputed from some point onward.
anchor.nothingNew: The chain head has not moved, so no new anchor was signed — signing the same position ten times adds nothing. Sign again after new audit entries appear.
anchor.mismatch: ⚠️ Anchor at entry {{seq}} does not match the current chain. The signature is valid, so the anchor itself was not altered; the mismatch means the audit chain was rewritten after that anchor was signed. This is exactly what anchors exist to catch.
anchor.exportWhy: {{total}} anchors, {{exported}} marked as exported. ⚠️ Anchors kept inside this system's own database protect nothing — whoever can rewrite the chain can also alter the anchor table. Store the exported file outside this system (object storage, email, a ticket, a third-party notary); that step is where anchoring actually starts working.

routes.title: Gateway routes
routes.desc: Which hostname's traffic goes to which backend, and which application's policy decides access. This is the step gateway proxying (zero-change onboarding) cannot skip — without a route the gateway does not know who owns that hostname.
routes.deleteWarn: Deleting this route leaves that hostname with nothing serving it
routes.notGatewayApp: That application uses {{type}}; its traffic does not pass through the gateway
routes.fHostHint: The hostname users' browsers hit. Host (and optional port) only — no http:// and no path. A hostname can have only one route, globally.
routes.fUpstreamHint: The machine actually serving it, e.g. http://10.42.6.31:3000. http:// is added if you omit it.
routes.fAppHint: Whether someone gets in follows this application's policies; which endpoints they may call follows its endpoint rules.
routes.reloadHint: ⚠️ Takes up to 30 seconds: the gateway reloads its route table every 30s (hot reload, no restart — restarting the gateway means a company-wide outage). Wait a moment before testing.

empty.title: No gateway routes yet
empty.reason: Applications connected via gateway proxying need a route here before the gateway knows the hostname belongs to them. OIDC applications do not — their traffic never passes through the gateway.

onboard.title: Onboarding · {{name}}
onboard.intro: Every value here comes from the running process and every tick from what is actually in the database — this is not documentation. Handbooks go stale, and the three things that stall an onboarding are all values: a mistyped issuer, a redirect URI off by one character, a client_id that does not match.
onboard.issuerLocal: 🔴 The current issuer is {{issuer}}, which points at this machine. Downstream systems fetch that address from inside their own container, where localhost means themselves — so nothing external can connect, and the error only ever shows up on their side. Set OAP_ISSUER to an address they can reach (a LAN IP is fine for local testing).
onboard.notSupported: This application uses {{type}}; there is no onboarding guide for it yet.
onboard.o1none: No client yet. Create one under OIDC clients for this application — without it the other side cannot even start a login.
onboard.o1secret: The client_secret is shown once at creation. If it was not saved, the client must be recreated — only a hash is stored.
onboard.o2: Redirect URI matches exactly what the other side registers
onboard.o2hint: One character off (a trailing slash, http vs https, a port) and it is rejected — and their error will not point back here. This is where onboarding most often stalls.
onboard.o3hint: Right now nobody can get into this application. With no allow rule the default is deny — the other side completes the login and is turned away immediately. Add a rule under Policies for the people or groups who should get in.
onboard.o4: Fill these in on the other system
onboard.o4hint: Copy these values directly. ⚠️ Whether they are entered correctly is invisible to us — that machine is not ours, so only you can confirm this step.
onboard.secretOnce: the string shown when the client was created
onboard.noRefresh: ⚠️ We do not issue refresh tokens (deliberately: an offline-renewable token bypasses session revocation and offboarding). So leave offline_access out of the scope for now. If the other system genuinely depends on it and errors, tell us — that needs rethinking what sign-out means, not a quick extra field.
onboard.rawTitle: Raw endpoints (the three lines downstream needs)
onboard.rawHint: These are the values this process is actually running with. The other side fetches discovery and the keys from its own network, so this address must be reachable from there.
onboard.g1none: No route yet. Add one under Gateway routes below: which hostname's traffic goes to which backend. Without it the gateway does not know the hostname belongs here.
onboard.g1hint: Changes take up to 30 seconds (the gateway hot-reloads).
onboard.g3none: ⚠️ With none at all, every request is denied (default deny) — even though Policies says the user has access. Add a /** allow as a catch-all first, then tighten.
onboard.g4: Point the hostname at the gateway
onboard.g4hint: Resolve the public hostname to the gateway in DNS / Ingress / Istio. ⚠️ That step lives outside this system so we cannot verify it — but without it traffic never reaches the gateway at all.
onboard.trafficNone: ⚠️ No access or login attempt has ever been recorded. That means traffic is not reaching us yet — check the other system's configuration, DNS and network reachability, not the policies here. “Configured but nobody came” and “they came and were denied” are entirely different problems.
onboard.trafficSome: {{n}} recorded, {{denied}} denied, most recent {{at}}. Traffic proves the path works — if people still cannot get in, it is a policy question; check Access audit for the exact rule that denied them.
onboard.o3ok: {{n}} of {{total}} people can currently get in. This is the result of actually running the evaluation, not a count of configured rules.
onboard.o3unavailable: Could not compute how many people have access — that is an API problem, not evidence that nothing is configured. Do not change policies based on this.

issuerHost.title: You are on a different host than the issuer
issuerHost.body: Sessions are stored per host. Signing in at {{current}} only creates a session for that address, while downstream apps are sent to {{issuer}} to log in — where that session does not exist, so you get asked to sign in again.
